name: St. Matilda
title: Queen of Germany, widow, founder
summary: Matilda was a tenth-century Saxon noblewoman who married Henry the Fowler, king of Germany, and raised five children, among them the Emperor Otto. After Henry died her sons quarreled over the crown and turned on her, and in the end they were reconciled. She is a patron of parents of large families and of widows, and a saint of the German world the abbey came from.
life: Matilda was born in Westphalia, in northern Germany, into a noble Saxon family that claimed descent from Widukind, the Saxon leader who had fought Charlemagne. She was brought up by her grandmother, the abbess of the convent at Herford, and there she learned to read and to pray the psalms. About 909 she married Henry, duke of the Saxons, who in 919 became king of Germany and is remembered as Henry the Fowler.

The marriage was a happy one and lasted twenty-seven years. They had five children. Otto became king and later emperor, Henry became duke of Bavaria, Bruno became archbishop of Cologne and is honored as a saint, and their daughters Gerberga and Hedwig married into the great houses of France. Her early biographers say that as queen she visited the sick, gave to the poor, and was known for getting up at night to pray.

When Henry died in 936, the family split. Matilda is said to have favored her younger son Henry for the crown, and when Otto was chosen the brothers were rivals for years. Both sons then turned on their mother. They accused her of draining the royal treasury with her gifts to the poor and to churches, had her followed and her accounts checked, and pushed her out of court. She withdrew to her estates in Westphalia. The story is that Otto's wife, the English princess Edith, persuaded him to call her back, and mother and sons were reconciled.

Matilda used her wealth to found religious houses. The most important was Quedlinburg, a community of noblewomen founded in 936 beside her husband's grave, which became one of the great houses of medieval Germany. She also founded houses at Nordhausen, Enger and Pöhlde. In her last years she lived mostly at Quedlinburg, and she died there on 14 March 968 and was buried beside Henry.

Two lives of her were written within about fifty years of her death, both by people close to her family, and they read partly as family history. The outline of her life, her marriage, her children, the quarrel and her foundations, is well attested. The label "S. Mehtildis" gives an old German spelling of her name and tells her apart from the later nuns St. Mechtild of Hackeborn and Mechtild of Magdeburg.
patronage: parents troubled by their children's quarrels
why_here: Matilda is a saint for parents. She raised five children who became powerful, watched two of them quarrel over a crown, and then had both turn against her. She did not stop loving them, and in the end they came back. Families who send a son or daughter to St. Bernard Prep, some from far away, know that raising a teenager can bring hard years as well as proud ones. Her prayers fit them well.

She also belongs to the German world from which the abbey came. Her foundations were houses of women living under a common life of prayer, and she spent her widowhood near one of them. Her generosity was called waste by people who counted the money. That is a quiet comfort for benefactors who give to a monastery and a school.
relic: One relic in the gold oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labeled "S. Mehtildis".
check: The catalogue's saint paragraph gives the label as "S. Mehtildis R.", but the photo table reads only "S. Mehtildis"; please check whether an "R." (Regina) is on the label. The patronage "parents troubled by their children's quarrels" is a popular one, not official.

name: St. Matthew
title: Apostle and evangelist
summary: Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum who got up from his booth when Jesus said, "Follow me." Very early tradition names him as the writer of the first Gospel, though scholars still argue the question, and later stories of his preaching and death are legend. He is the patron of tax collectors and accountants, and so of everyone at the abbey and the Prep who keeps the books.
life: Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee. Men like him bought the right to collect tolls and customs for the rulers and kept what they could take above that. His neighbors would have counted him a collaborator and a cheat, and the Gospels group tax collectors with sinners as a matter of course. Mark and Luke call him Levi, and Mark adds that he was the son of Alphaeus.

The call is told in one sentence. Jesus saw him sitting at the tax booth and said, "Follow me," and he got up and followed him (Matthew 9:9). Luke adds that Matthew left everything and then gave a great banquet in his house for Jesus, with a crowd of tax collectors and others at the table. When the Pharisees complained, Jesus answered that the sick need a doctor, not the healthy, and that he came to call sinners.

Very early tradition names Matthew as the writer of the first Gospel. Papias, a bishop of the early second century, wrote that Matthew put together the sayings of Jesus in the Hebrew language. Many scholars today think the Greek Gospel we have was written later, perhaps by a disciple who drew on Mark, and the question is still argued. The Gospel itself is written for readers who knew the Jewish Scriptures. It quotes the prophets again and again and gathers the teaching of Jesus into great sermons, among them the Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer.

After the list of the Twelve and the account of Pentecost, the New Testament says nothing more about him. Later traditions disagree. Some say he preached among the Jews of Palestine, others in Ethiopia, Persia or Parthia, and accounts of his martyrdom are late and legendary. Since the tenth century the cathedral of Salerno, in southern Italy, has claimed his body, and it is venerated in the crypt there. In art he is shown with a winged man, the first of the four creatures of Revelation 4, because his Gospel opens with the human ancestry of Jesus.
The label "Ex Os. S. Mathei Ap." means "from the bone of St. Matthew, Apostle".
why_here: A monastery has accounts like any other house. Someone has to pay the bills, keep the books, sell the bread and handle what benefactors give. St. Benedict asks the cellarer to treat the goods of the monastery as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar. Matthew, the man who left the tax table, is a good patron for the procurator and for everyone at the abbey and the Prep whose work is money and records.

His call also speaks to students. Matthew was not chosen because he was respectable. He was chosen where he sat, and he answered. For young people working out what to do with their lives, that short sentence is worth keeping.
relic: One relic on the large grey linen board, labeled "Ex Os. S. Mathei Ap.".

name: St. Maurice
title: Soldier and martyr
summary: Maurice is honored as the commander of the Theban Legion, Christian soldiers said to have been put to death at Agaunum, in the Alps, for refusing an order of the emperor. Christian soldiers probably were martyred there, but a whole legion killed at once is very likely legend. He is the patron of soldiers, fitting for an abbey whose monks served as military chaplains.
life: The story of St. Maurice comes from a letter written about 440 by Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, some 150 years after the events. He says he heard it from people who had it from earlier witnesses. The Theban Legion, a unit of Christian soldiers raised in Upper Egypt, was marched over the Alps to serve the Emperor Maximian. At Agaunum, in the Rhône valley of what is now Switzerland, the emperor ordered the army to sacrifice to the gods, and in some versions to kill Christians of the area. The Theban soldiers refused.

According to Eucherius, Maximian had the legion decimated, every tenth man killed, and when the rest still refused he had it done again. Maurice, the commander, with his officers Exuperius and Candidus, encouraged the men to stand firm. They said they owed the emperor their service as soldiers but owed God their innocence, and they would not use their weapons against fellow believers. In the end the whole legion was put to death without resistance.

Historians think there probably were Christian soldiers martyred at Agaunum, and that their tomb was honored there by the late fourth century. But a whole legion of over six thousand men killed at once is very likely legend, and nothing outside this tradition confirms it. The story spread, and other martyrs in the Rhineland and northern Italy, among them the martyrs of Trier whose relics the abbey also keeps, were later tied to the same legion.

In 515 King Sigismund of Burgundy founded a monastery over the tomb at Agaunum, now the town of Saint-Maurice. Its monks kept up the laus perennis, the "unceasing praise", with choirs taking turns so that the psalms never stopped day or night. A religious community, today of canons regular, has lived there ever since, one of the oldest in the West. Maurice became a patron of soldiers and of the Holy Roman Empire. The Emperor Otto I dedicated his new monastery at Magdeburg to him in 937, and from the thirteenth century he was often shown in German art as a Black African, a reminder of the legion's Egyptian origin.
The label "s. Mauritii M." means "of St. Maurice, Martyr".
patronage: Piedmont and the House of Savoy
why_here: Monks of St. Bernard Abbey served as military chaplains in both world wars and in Korea, and some Prep graduates go on to serve in uniform. Maurice is the patron of soldiers, and the core of his story is the hardest part of a soldier's life, being loyal to one's commanders and still refusing an order that conscience forbids. That is worth praying about for anyone who serves.

The monastery built over his tomb is also a reminder of what monks do. Its choirs kept praise going without a break. At Cullman the monks gather in choir five times a day, from Matins at dawn to Compline at night. It is the same work on a smaller scale.
relic: One relic in the large pewter-colored oval of fifteen relics, labeled "s. Mauritii M.".
check: "Patronage of Piedmont and the House of Savoy" rests on the Savoyard Order of Sts. Maurice and Lazarus; drop it if a simpler list is wanted.

name: St. Nicholas of Bari
title: Bishop of Myra, friend of children
summary: Nicholas was a fourth-century bishop of Myra, in what is now Turkey, and most of what is told of him, like the three bags of gold for poor girls' dowries, is legend. His bones have rested at Bari since 1087. He is the patron of children and schoolboys and of sailors, and a good friend for the Prep's students and the monks who teach them.
life: Nicholas was bishop of Myra, a port town in Lycia, on the south coast of what is now Turkey, in the fourth century. That he lived, that he was bishop there, and that he was honored very early are history. Nearly everything else told of him comes from lives written centuries later, and is legend. Tradition says he was born at nearby Patara to wealthy Christian parents, gave away his inheritance, and suffered in the persecution under Diocletian. A later story puts him at the Council of Nicaea in 325, but his name is not on the oldest lists of the bishops there.

The oldest story about him is of three army officers falsely condemned to death, whom Nicholas saved by appearing to the emperor in a dream. The best known is of a poor man with three daughters and no money for their dowries, who was about to give them up to a life of shame. Nicholas went by night three times and threw a bag of gold through the window, so the girls could marry. A medieval legend tells that he brought back to life three boys, students in some versions, killed by an innkeeper. Those stories made him the patron of children and schoolboys, of brides, and of the falsely accused, and stories of storms calmed made him the patron of sailors.

His cult spread through the Greek East and then through Russia, where he is among the most loved of all saints. In 1087 sailors from Bari, in southern Italy, took his bones from Myra, then under threat from the Seljuk Turks, and carried them home. The great basilica of San Nicola was built over them, and they have rested at Bari ever since. A clear liquid that gathers in the tomb, the "manna" of St. Nicholas, is collected each year.

In the Low Countries and Germany, children came to expect gifts from Nicholas on his feast or its eve. Dutch settlers brought Sinterklaas to New York, and from him came the American Santa Claus. The gift-giver has drifted far from the bishop, but the line runs back to the story of the three bags of gold.
The catalogue reads his label as "S. Nicol. Bar.", "of St. Nicholas of Bari", naming him by the city that keeps his body.
why_here: Nicholas is the name saint of Br. Nicholas, one of the novices. He is also, by long tradition, the patron of children and of schoolboys. The Prep's students are teenagers, some of them living away from their families for the first time. A bishop remembered for looking out for the young and for the poor, quietly and without being thanked, is a good friend for them and for the monks who teach them.

Cullman was founded by German immigrants, and the German custom of gifts on St. Nicholas Day was one of the ways his feast came to America. The story behind it is about giving in secret to people in need.
relic: One relic in the gold oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labeled "S. Nicol. Bar." in the catalogue.
check: The photo table reads this label only as "[S.] Nicol. [...]"; the catalogue's saint paragraph reads "S. Nicol. Bar.". Please confirm "Bar." on the relic.

name: St. Norbert
title: Founder of the Premonstratensians, archbishop
summary: Norbert was a comfortable canon at Xanten who, after a lightning strike threw him from his horse in 1115, gave away his property and became a barefoot preacher. He founded the Premonstratensians, or Norbertines, at Prémontré and died archbishop of Magdeburg in 1134. He is the patron of his order and of Magdeburg, and he was a friend and ally of St. Bernard, the abbey's patron.
life: Norbert was born at Xanten, on the Lower Rhine, into a noble family. As a young man he became a canon of the church at Xanten and was ordained subdeacon, which gave him an income without the duties of a priest. He spent time at the court of the archbishop of Cologne and of the Emperor Henry V, and he lived well. His early life story says that in 1115, riding in a thunderstorm near Vreden, he was thrown from his horse by a lightning strike and lay unconscious for an hour. When he came to, he asked what God wanted of him and heard, "Turn from evil and do good."

He took the warning seriously. He was ordained priest, did penance, gave away his property, and tried to reform the canons at Xanten, who did not want to be reformed. In 1118 he got leave from the pope to preach wherever he went, and he walked barefoot through northern France and the Low Countries, making peace between feuding families and calling people to conversion.

In 1120 the bishop of Laon gave him a lonely valley at Prémontré. At Christmas 1121 Norbert and his first companions made their profession there under the Rule of St. Augustine. They were canons, priests living in common and serving the people around them, with a life of prayer and penance close to that of monks. Pope Honorius II approved the order in 1126, and the Premonstratensians, or Norbertines, spread quickly across Europe. In Antwerp he worked against the preacher Tanchelm, who had taught that the sacraments were worthless, and in art Norbert often holds a monstrance for this reason.

Also in 1126 he was made archbishop of Magdeburg, on the eastern edge of the German lands. He set about reforming the clergy and recovering church property, and he made enemies, who once tried to kill him. He was a friend of St. Bernard of Clairvaux. In the papal schism of 1130 both men worked hard for Pope Innocent II. Norbert died at Magdeburg on 6 June 1134. He was canonized in 1582, and in 1627 his body was moved to the Strahov monastery in Prague.
The label "Ex ossibus S. Norberti Ep. Conf." means "from the bones of Saint Norbert, Bishop and Confessor".
why_here: Norbert was a friend and ally of St. Bernard, the abbey's patron. The two men were part of the same great reform of the twelfth century, one founding Cistercian houses and the other houses of canons, both trying to bring religious life back to poverty, prayer and common life. It is fitting that his relic sits in the house of Bernard's monks.

His story is also one of a comfortable man who came to himself. He held a church post for the income and lived at court, until one storm made him ask what God wanted. The question he asked is the one young people at the Prep are learning to ask, and the one every monk asked before he came to Cullman.
relic: One relic in the set of jewelled gilt reliquaries, labeled "Ex ossibus S. Norberti Ep. Conf.".
check: Patronages "Bohemia" and "a safe childbirth" are traditional (Bohemia since the translation to Prague) but worth a check.

name: St. Oswald
title: King of Northumbria and martyr
summary: Oswald was a seventh-century king of Northumbria who learned the faith in exile with the monks of Iona. As king he brought St. Aidan to Lindisfarne, translated his sermons himself, and gave his own silver dish to the poor, as St. Bede tells. He was killed in battle in 642. He is a patron of Northumbria and of kings, and a model of the bond between monks and lay people.
life: Almost all we know of Oswald comes from St. Bede, who wrote his Ecclesiastical History of the English People about ninety years after Oswald's death and drew on people who remembered him. Oswald was a son of Æthelfrith, the pagan king of Northumbria in the north of England. When his father was killed in 616 and a rival, Edwin, took the throne, the boy fled north with his brothers. He grew up in exile among the Irish of western Scotland, and with the monks of Iona, the monastery founded by St. Columba, he became a Christian and was baptized.

In 633 Edwin was killed, and the Welsh king Cadwallon laid Northumbria waste. Oswald came back with a small army. Before the battle at Heavenfield, near Hexham, in 634, he had a wooden cross made and set it up himself, holding it while his men filled in the hole, and he had them kneel and pray. He won the battle and the kingdom. Adomnán of Iona adds that St. Columba had appeared to him in a dream the night before.

Oswald asked Iona for a bishop to teach his people. The first monk sent found the English stubborn and went home. The second was St. Aidan, who settled on the island of Lindisfarne in 635. Aidan did not yet speak English, so the king himself, who had learned Irish in exile, translated his sermons for his nobles. Bede tells that one Easter, as Oswald sat at dinner, he was told that the poor were gathered outside. He sent them his food and had the silver dish broken up and shared among them. Aidan, sitting with him, took his right hand and said, "May this hand never perish."

After eight years as king, Oswald was killed in battle against the pagan Penda of Mercia at Maserfield in 642. Bede says he died praying for the souls of his soldiers. Penda had his head and arms cut off and set on stakes. His brother Oswiu recovered them a year later. His head was placed with St. Cuthbert, and it lies in Cuthbert's tomb at Durham to this day. Bede says the right arm was kept at Bamburgh and did not decay. His cult spread to the continent, and he became popular in Germany and the Alpine lands.
The label "S. Oswaldi R." means "of St. Oswald, King".
patronage: the town and canton of Zug, Switzerland
why_here: Oswald's story comes from St. Bede, the name saint of Fr. Bede, the prior. It is also a story about what a monastery can give a layman and what he can give back. He learned the faith from the monks of Iona as an exile. When he became king he sent for them, gave them land, and stood beside Aidan as his interpreter. The abbey's oblates, lay men and women attached to the monastery, live a version of that bond.

The silver dish is the other lesson. Oswald was a warrior king, and the thing remembered of his hands is that he gave away his own table's silver. Students who play hard and want to win can find in him a hero who was both brave and generous.
relic: One relic in the gold oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labeled "S. Oswaldi R.".
check: Patronage of Zug is traditional (St. Oswald's church there) but please confirm before publishing.

name: St. Pacificus of San Severino
title: Franciscan friar and preacher
summary: Pacificus was an Italian Franciscan friar who preached missions to the farmers and shepherds of the hills around San Severino. Illness left him lame, nearly deaf and almost blind, and for more than thirty years he lived as an invalid, praying and receiving those who asked his help. He is a patron of San Severino, and a fitting one for the abbey's old and sick monks.
life: He was born Carlo Antonio Divini at San Severino in the Marche, the hill country of central Italy, in 1653. His parents died when he was a small child, and he was raised by an uncle, a priest, whose house was strict and unkind. At seventeen he entered the Franciscan friars of the Observance, the branch that kept the stricter life, and took the name Pacificus.

He was ordained priest in 1678 and for a time taught philosophy to the young friars. His real work, though, was preaching. He went out to the villages of the mountains around San Severino and preached simple missions to farmers and shepherds, and he was much sought after as a confessor. He lived poorly and was hard on himself.

When he was about thirty-five, a long illness changed everything. He became lame, nearly deaf and almost blind, and could no longer travel or preach. He was moved first to a friary nearby and then to the friary of Santa Maria delle Grazie at San Severino. For more than thirty years he lived there as an invalid, praying long hours, saying Mass when he could, and receiving the people who came to ask his prayers and advice. For a time he served as guardian, the superior of the house. Those who knew him spoke of his patience and of his long times of prayer, and stories of prophecies and cures gathered around him, as they did around many holy people of his time.
He died at San Severino on 24 September 1721. He was beatified in 1786 and canonized by Pope Gregory XVI in 1839, and his body is venerated in his town.
The label in the Franciscan reliquary reads "B. Pacifici a S. Sev..." and calls him Blessed. With the other labels there, it dates that reliquary to between 1825 and 1839.
why_here: Most of Pacificus's life as a friar was spent not doing the work he had been trained for. Illness took his legs, his ears and his eyes, and he spent three decades in one house praying and listening. The abbey keeps an infirmary for its old and sick monks, men who once taught, coached, built and preached and now pray in a quieter way. He is a patron for them and for the brothers who care for them.
He was also an orphan raised in a hard home, who still became a gentle man. Some students carry hard things from home with them. His life says that this need not decide who they become.
relic: One relic in the Gothic gilt reliquary of Franciscan saints, labeled "B. Pacifici a S. Sev[erino]" (handwritten and faint).
check: The label is faint and read as "likely". His uncle being a priest and his service as guardian are from standard modern lives; confirm if they are to be kept.

name: St. Patrick
title: Bishop, apostle of Ireland
summary: Patrick was a Briton carried off to Ireland as a slave at sixteen, where he learned to pray, and who later went back as a bishop to the Irish. We know him from his own Confession, while the shamrock and the snakes are later legends. He is the patron of Ireland and of the Irish abroad, and a companion for Prep boarders far from home.
life: Patrick is one of the few early saints we can hear in his own voice. Two short works of his survive, the Confession, written near the end of his life to defend his mission, and a Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus, a British warlord whose men had killed and enslaved some of his new converts. Nearly everything reliable about him comes from these two texts.

He was born in Roman Britain. His father, Calpornius, was a deacon and a town official, and his grandfather, Potitus, was a priest. He says that as a boy he did not really know God. At about sixteen he was seized by Irish raiders from his father's small estate and taken to Ireland as a slave, where he herded animals for six years. There, alone in the woods and on the mountain in snow and rain, he began to pray, as many as a hundred times a day and as many at night. A voice in a dream told him a ship was ready, and he walked some two hundred miles to the coast, found it, and got home.

Years later, he writes, he dreamed of a man named Victoricus bringing letters from Ireland, and heard "the voice of the Irish" begging him to come and walk among them again. He trained for the priesthood, though where is not certain, and returned to Ireland as a bishop. He baptized many, ordained clergy, encouraged men and women to give their lives to God, and lived with the risk of being robbed, imprisoned and killed. He was often ashamed of his poor Latin and his broken education, and he says so plainly. "I, Patrick, a sinner, a very simple countryman," the Confession begins.

His exact dates are not known. The traditional dates, coming to Ireland in 432 and dying in 461 or 493, are later reckonings, and scholars still argue them. The shamrock used to explain the Trinity, the driving out of the snakes and the fire on the hill of Slane are later legends. Downpatrick, in the north of Ireland, claims his grave.
The label "Oss. S. Pat. Ep." means "from the bones of Saint Pat., Bishop". "Pat." is most likely Patrick, though the abbreviation alone cannot rule out another bishop with a similar name.
why_here: St. Patrick is the name saint of Fr. Patrick. He is also the saint of a teenager taken far from home. He was sixteen, alone, among strangers whose language he did not speak, and that was where he learned to pray. Prep boarders are not captives, but many are a long way from their families, and the first months can be lonely. Patrick shows that such a time can become the start of a real life with God.

He also wrote honestly about his weak schooling. He knew others were better educated and he was embarrassed by it, but he wrote anyway because he had something true to say. Students who struggle with their studies can take heart from him.
relic: One relic on the large grey linen board, labeled "Oss. S. Pat. Ep." (read as Patrick, likely).
check: The label "Pat." is read as Patrick but could be another bishop; the authentica would settle it.

name: St. Paul of the Cross
title: Priest, founder of the Passionists
feast: 19 October (20 October in the United States)
summary: Paul of the Cross was an Italian priest of the eighteenth century who founded the Passionists, vowed to keep alive the memory of Christ's Passion. His houses, which he called retreats, sent preachers to the poor of the countryside, and his letters show that he kept praying through many dry years. He is the patron of the Passionists, and a natural one for the abbey's Retreat Center.
life: Paolo Francesco Danei was born at Ovada in Liguria, northern Italy, in 1694, the eldest surviving child of a merchant family that had come down in the world. He had little schooling. He helped his father in the business, taught the catechism, and at about nineteen went through what he called his conversion, a turn to a life of strict prayer and penance. For a while he thought of joining a crusade against the Turks, then gave the idea up.

In 1720, after visions of himself clothed in a black habit with a sign of the Passion on the breast, he spent forty days alone in a tiny room beside a church at Castellazzo, and there he wrote a rule for a new community. Its members would add to the usual vows a fourth one, to keep alive the memory of Christ's Passion and teach others to do the same. With his brother John Baptist, who stayed with him all his life, he went to Rome, nursed the sick in a hospital, and was ordained priest by Pope Benedict XIII in 1727.

The two brothers settled on Monte Argentario, a rocky headland on the Tuscan coast, and in 1737 opened the first house there. Paul called his houses "retreats". The religious lived in solitude and prayer, and from there went out to preach missions, often in the malarial marshes of the Maremma, to poor country people whom few others reached. Pope Benedict XIV approved the rule in 1741, and the Passionists grew slowly, held back by poverty and opposition. In 1771 Paul also founded a community of Passionist nuns.

His many letters, of which some two thousand survive, show a gifted spiritual director. They also show that for many years, by some accounts close to fifty, he felt almost no comfort in his own prayer, and kept on anyway. He spent his last years in Rome at the church of Sts. John and Paul, which Pope Clement XIV gave to the order, and died there on 18 October 1775. He was beatified in 1853 and canonized in 1867. St. Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows, whose relics are also at the abbey, was one of his Passionists.
The label "S. Pauli a Cruce" means "of St. Paul of the Cross".
why_here: Paul of the Cross was a man of retreats. He wanted houses set apart, quiet and plain, where people could pray and from which preachers went out. St. Bernard Abbey has run a Retreat and Conference Center since 1981, and he is a natural patron for the people who come there to step out of ordinary life for a few days, and for the monks who receive them.

His long dryness in prayer matters too. Monks pray the Office every day for their whole lives, and many years of it can feel flat. Paul kept faith with prayer that gave him nothing he could feel, and he is a companion for anyone who does the same.
relic: One relic in a sunburst stand, labeled "S. Pauli a Cruce".
check: The 20 October date is the U.S. calendar's (19 October being Sts. Isaac Jogues and John de Brébeuf there). The figure of about two thousand surviving letters and the length of his dryness are approximate.

name: St. Paul the Apostle
title: Apostle to the Gentiles
summary: Paul, born Saul at Tarsus, hunted the followers of Jesus until he met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. He spent some thirty years founding churches around the Mediterranean, wrote letters that are the oldest Christian writings we have, and was put to death in Rome. He is the patron of missionaries and of tentmakers, and a fitting one for monks who live by prayer and work.
life: Paul, whose Jewish name was Saul, was born at Tarsus, a Greek-speaking city in what is now southern Turkey, and was a Roman citizen by birth. He was trained as a Pharisee, strict in keeping the Law, and by trade he was a tentmaker. As a young man he took part in hunting down the followers of Jesus in Jerusalem, and he was present, the Acts of the Apostles says, when St. Stephen was stoned.

On the road to Damascus, about the year 34, he was stopped by a light from heaven and a voice that said, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" Blinded, he was led into the city and baptized. He always spoke of this as a meeting with the risen Jesus, who had made him an apostle, the last and least of them, as he put it.

For some thirty years he travelled the eastern Mediterranean on foot and by ship, preaching first in the synagogues and then to the Gentiles. He founded churches in Galatia, Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth and Ephesus, and argued, against strong opposition, that Gentile believers did not have to be circumcised or keep the whole Jewish Law. He supported himself by the work of his hands so that he would not be a burden on anyone. He kept in touch with his churches by letter, and thirteen letters in the New Testament bear his name. Scholars agree that at least seven are his own, and they are the oldest Christian writings we have.

His life was hard. He lists it himself in his Second Letter to the Corinthians: flogged five times, beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, often hungry, cold and in danger. Arrested in Jerusalem, he appealed as a citizen to the emperor and was taken to Rome as a prisoner, surviving a shipwreck on Malta on the way. Acts ends with him under house arrest in Rome, preaching freely.

What happened next is not in the Bible. Early tradition, already known to St. Clement of Rome about 96, says he was put to death in Rome under Nero. As a citizen he would have been beheaded. His tomb is honored at the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.
why_here: Paul worked with his hands while he preached. He reminded the Thessalonians that he had worked night and day so as not to burden them, and he wrote that whoever will not work should not eat. Benedictines live by prayer and work, and the abbey's builders, carvers, potter, bakers and farmers are in good company with the tentmaker of Tarsus.

He also wrote for athletes. He told the Corinthians that runners in a race train hard for a prize that fades, and that he ran so as to win one that does not. Prep students who run, play and lift can find their training in his letters.
relic: Two relics: one in the square theca in the velvet case, labeled "s. Pauli Apos.", and one in the large pewter-colored oval, labeled "s. Pauli. Apos".

name: St. Peter the Apostle
title: First of the apostles
summary: Simon Peter was a fisherman of Galilee whom Jesus named the rock and set first among the Twelve. He denied Jesus three times, was forgiven, and was given his flock to feed. Strong early tradition says he was put to death in Rome under Nero. He is the patron of the popes and the universal Church, and a saint of second chances for students, monks and the abbey's new abbot.
life: Simon, son of John, was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee. He came from Bethsaida and lived at Capernaum, where Jesus healed his mother-in-law, so he was a married man. He worked the boats with his brother Andrew and with James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Jesus called him from his nets and gave him a new name, Cephas in Aramaic, Petros in Greek, meaning "rock".

The Gospels give him the first place among the Twelve. He is named first in every list, he speaks for the others, and at Caesarea Philippi he is the one who says, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus answers that on this rock he will build his church and gives him the keys of the kingdom. Yet the Gospels are frank about his failings. He sank when he tried to walk on the water, tried to talk Jesus out of the cross and was called Satan for it, fell asleep in Gethsemane, and on the night of the arrest denied three times that he even knew him. After the resurrection Jesus asked him three times, "Do you love me?" and three times gave him his flock to feed.

In the Acts of the Apostles Peter leads the church in Jerusalem. He preaches on Pentecost, heals in the name of Jesus, is jailed and set free, and opens the church to the Gentiles by baptizing the Roman officer Cornelius. Paul writes that he went to Jerusalem to see Peter and later argued with him at Antioch over eating with Gentiles. Two letters in the New Testament bear his name.

Early and strong tradition says he went to Rome and was put to death there under Nero, about 64. St. Clement of Rome, writing about 96, speaks of his martyrdom, and the tradition that he was crucified, and asked to be crucified head down, is told by Origen. A small shrine over his grave on the Vatican hill was honored by the second century, and Constantine built the first St. Peter's over it. Excavations beneath the basilica in the 1940s found that shrine, and in 1968 Pope Paul VI said that bones found there were, in the Church's judgment, very probably Peter's.
why_here: Peter is the saint of the second chance. He made bold promises and broke them, and he wept and was forgiven, and then he was trusted with more. Teenagers fail, sometimes publicly. So do monks and teachers. A school and a monastery both need the kind of forgiveness that Jesus gave Peter on the beach, the kind that ends with a task, not just a pardon.

He is also a patron for those who lead. St. Benedict says the abbot holds the place of Christ in the monastery and must account for every soul. In 2026 the monks elected a new abbot. Peter, who led because he was asked to and not because he had never fallen, is good to pray to for him.
relic: Three relics: one in the large oval in the velvet case ("S. Petri Ap."), one in the square theca in the same case ("s. Petri Apos."), and one in the large pewter-colored oval ("s. Petri Apos").

name: A St. Philip
title: A Philip not yet identified
summary: This relic is a large piece of bone with the name inked on it, and only "S. Phili…" can be read, so the label cannot tell us which St. Philip is meant. The strongest candidates are Philip the Apostle, Philip Neri and Philip Benizi. The abbey honors it as it is, a saint known to God, and a small puzzle for a patient eye.
life: This is a large piece of bone with the name inked straight onto it, an older practice than a paper label. Only "S." and "Phili…" can be read, and a worn word between them may once have said which Philip is meant. Several saints of that name had relics given out widely.

The strongest candidates are St. Philip the Apostle (feast 3 May), one of the Twelve, whose relics are honored in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome; St. Philip Neri (26 May), the founder of the Roman Oratory, whose relic in a separate pendant is also at the abbey; and St. Philip Benizi (23 August), a thirteenth-century Servite friar from Florence who led his order and is said to have fled from being made pope. Other Philips, such as the martyr St. Philip of Heraclea, are possible but less likely. A look at the bone in good, raking light, with a lamp held low and to one side, might bring out the missing word, and any surviving authentication papers would settle it.
why_here: Not every relic comes with its story intact. This one has kept a saint's name and lost the rest. It is honest to leave it so and to honor it anyway, trusting that the saint is known to God even when the label has faded. It is also a small piece of work waiting for a patient eye, the sort of puzzle a careful student or monk might one day solve.
relic: One large piece of bone in a jewelled gilt reliquary, the name inked on it: "S. … Phili…" (worn; which Philip is unsure).
check: Which Philip is unknown. Try raking light on the bone and look for an authentica.

name: St. Philip Neri
title: Priest, founder of the Oratory, "Apostle of Rome"
summary: Philip Neri was a Florentine who spent his life in Rome, talking with young men in its streets, hearing confessions for hours, and founding the Congregation of the Oratory. He was famous for his humor, which he used to keep himself and others humble. He is a patron of Rome and of joy, and a good one for teachers, coaches and dorm staff at the Prep.
life: Philip Neri was born in Florence in 1515, the son of a notary, and as a boy he learned much from the Dominican friars of San Marco. At about eighteen he was sent to work for a relative in business at San Germano, the town at the foot of Monte Cassino. He did not stay. He went to Rome, about 1533, and remained there for the rest of his life.

For years he lived as a layman in a small room, tutoring the sons of a Florentine family in return for his keep. He studied philosophy and theology for a time, then sold his books and gave the money to the poor. By day he talked with young men in the streets, shops and banks of Rome, and by night he prayed in the churches and in the catacombs. In 1544, praying in the catacomb of St. Sebastian at Pentecost, he felt what he described as a ball of fire enter his heart. For the rest of his life his heart beat so hard it could be seen, and after his death the doctors found it enlarged and two of his ribs pushed outward. In 1548 he helped start a confraternity to care for poor pilgrims.

He was ordained priest in 1551, at thirty-six, and heard confessions for hours every day. Young men gathered in his room for talks, reading, prayer and music, and the meetings outgrew it and moved to a room above a church, called the Oratory. The musical pieces sung there gave the "oratorio" its name. He led crowds on walking pilgrimages to the seven great churches of Rome, with a picnic and music on the way. In 1575 Pope Gregory XIII approved the Congregation of the Oratory, secular priests living together without vows, and gave them the church of Santa Maria in Vallicella.

Philip was famous for his humor. He wore his clothes inside out, went out with half his beard shaved, and gave his disciples silly tasks to keep them from vanity, and himself from being thought a saint. Popes, cardinals and the poor went to him for advice. St. Camillus de Lellis, whose relic is also at the abbey, was one of his penitents. He died on 26 May 1595 and was canonized in 1622, with Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila and Isidore the Farmer.
The label "Ex praecordiis" means "from the area of the heart".
why_here: Philip spent his life with young men. He did not lecture them from a distance. He met them where they were, played games, made music, joked, heard their confessions and took them out walking. Teachers, coaches and dorm staff at the Prep do much the same, and Philip is a good patron for anyone who has to be both an adult in charge and a friend to teenagers.
His humor was not a decoration. He used it to keep himself and others humble. A school that hopes to form a love of learning and a life of virtue needs that lightness too, and so does a monastery.
relic: One relic on the large grey linen board, in a gilt pendant shared with St. Catherine Labouré and St. John Vianney, labeled "Ex praecordiis S. Phil. Nerii".
check: The patronages "humorists" and "joy" are popular rather than official.

name: St. Philip the Apostle
title: One of the Twelve
summary: Philip was one of the Twelve, from Bethsaida in Galilee, and John's Gospel shows him bringing his friend Nathanael to Jesus with the words "Come and see." Tradition places his grave at Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, though the stories of his martyrdom are late. He is a patron of Uruguay and of hatters, and a fitting one for the abbey's growing vocations.
life: Philip came from Bethsaida, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, the town of Peter and Andrew. Matthew, Mark and Luke only name him in their lists of the Twelve, always fifth. It is John's Gospel that gives him a face, in four short scenes.

In the first, Jesus finds Philip and says, "Follow me," and Philip at once goes to find his friend Nathanael and tells him they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip does not argue. He says, "Come and see." In the second, before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus asks Philip where they could buy bread for the crowd, and Philip works out that two hundred days' wages would not buy enough for each to have a little. In the third, some Greeks come to Philip, perhaps because of his Greek name, and say, "Sir, we would like to see Jesus," and he takes them to Andrew and the two go to Jesus. In the fourth, at the Last Supper, Philip says, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us," and Jesus answers, "Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father."

After Pentecost he is named once more in Acts, and then he leaves the New Testament. About 190, Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, wrote that Philip "of the Twelve" was buried at Hierapolis in Phrygia, in western Turkey, with two of his daughters. Some scholars think Polycrates mixed him up with Philip the deacon in Acts, who also had daughters, and the two Philips were often confused in later tradition. Accounts of his martyrdom at Hierapolis, crucified in some versions, are late. In 2011 Italian archaeologists working at Hierapolis announced that they had found a tomb they believe to be his. Relics honored as his have long been kept in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome, with those of St. James the Less.
The label "Philippi Ap." means "of Philip the Apostle" and keeps him apart from Philip the deacon.
why_here: "Come and see" may be the best description of how vocations happen. Philip did not argue his friend into faith. He brought him to meet Jesus and let the meeting do the rest. Monks talk about their life that way, and families visiting the Prep are invited the same way. With vocations increasing at St. Bernard, Philip is a fitting patron for the monks who invite and for the young men who come to look.
He is also the apostle who did the arithmetic, worked out that it was not enough, and saw it become enough. That is a familiar experience in any house that lives on faith and a budget.
relic: One relic in the large oval in the velvet case, labeled "[S.] Philippi Ap." (likely; read from crops).
check: Label read as "likely". Patronage of hatters is traditional but minor.

name: St. Pier Giorgio Frassati
title: Student, mountaineer, friend of the poor
summary: Pier Giorgio Frassati was a young man of Turin who loved the mountains, his friends and a good joke, went to Mass every day, and quietly gave almost all he had to the poor. He died of polio in 1925 at twenty-four and was canonized in 2025. He is a patron of young people, students and athletes, the saint for the Prep's students as they are.
life: Pier Giorgio Frassati was born in Turin on 6 April 1901. His father, Alfredo, founded and ran the newspaper La Stampa, was a senator, and later served as Italy's ambassador to Germany. His mother, Adelaide, was a painter. The family was wealthy and not very religious, and the parents' marriage was unhappy. Pier Giorgio grew up devout almost on his own, going to Mass and Communion daily as a teenager.

He was not a brilliant student and had to repeat a year of school. He chose to study mining engineering at the Turin Polytechnic, he said, so that he could serve Christ among the miners, whose work was among the hardest and most dangerous in Italy. He joined Catholic student groups and Catholic Action, became a lay Dominican, and was active in politics, opposing the Fascists openly and once fighting off a gang of them who broke into his family home.

From the age of seventeen he belonged to the St. Vincent de Paul Society, and he spent much of his time and almost all his money on the poor of Turin. He visited their rooms, brought food, coal and medicine, paid rents, and often gave away his train fare and ran home. His family knew little of this. He also loved the mountains. He climbed and skied with his friends in the Alps, organized outings with Mass and prayer, and wrote "Verso l'alto", "to the heights", on a photograph of one of his climbs. Friends remembered his laughter and his pranks.

In the summer of 1925 he fell ill with polio, probably caught from someone he visited. The family was busy with his grandmother, who was dying, and no one realized how sick he was. In his last days, already paralyzed, he wrote a note asking a friend to bring medicine to a poor man. He died on 4 July 1925, aged twenty-four. At his funeral his family was astonished at the crowds of poor people lining the streets.

John Paul II beatified him in 1990 and called him "the man of the eight Beatitudes". He was canonized on 7 September 2025. The label "B. PIER GEOR. F." calls him Blessed, so it was written between those two dates.
why_here: Pier Giorgio is the saint for the Prep's students as they actually are. He was a teenager and a college student, not a great one in the classroom, who loved sports and his friends, played jokes, argued politics and went to Mass every day. He climbed mountains and he climbed the stairs of the poorest tenements in Turin, and he saw no conflict between the two.

For athletes, he shows that strength and competition can belong to a life of faith. For students far from home, he shows that holiness does not need anyone's permission or applause. Most of his charity was done in secret, and it was only at his funeral that his family learned who he had been.
relic: One relic in a gilt theca, labeled "B. PIER GEOR. F." (hand-lettered).
check: The repeated school year (usually said to be for failing Latin) is widely reported; confirm if kept. His patronage of athletes is popular, not formally declared.

name: St. Pius X
title: Pope, "pope of the Eucharist"
summary: Pius X was a poor village boy who became a parish priest, patriarch of Venice and, in 1903, pope. He called for the return of Gregorian chant and let children receive First Communion at about seven, though his campaign against Modernism harmed some loyal scholars. He is the patron of first communicants and catechists, and his causes are lived at St. Bernard every day.
life: Giuseppe Sarto was born on 2 June 1835 at Riese, a village near Treviso in the Venetian countryside, the second of ten children of the village postman and a seamstress. The family was poor. He walked miles each day to school, and a scholarship took him to the seminary at Padua. He was ordained in 1858.

He spent seventeen years as a parish priest, first as a curate at Tombolo and then as pastor at Salzano. He taught the catechism himself, started a night school for adults, and nursed the sick in a cholera outbreak. He then served in the seminary and the diocesan offices at Treviso, was made bishop of Mantua in 1884, and in 1893 became cardinal and patriarch of Venice. He never lost the manners of a country priest. In 1903, at the conclave after Leo XIII died, he was elected pope, much against his own wish, and took the name Pius. His motto was "to restore all things in Christ".

His reforms touched the daily life of Catholics. In 1903 he called for the return of Gregorian chant to the liturgy and asked that the people sing, drawing on the work of the Benedictine monks of Solesmes. In 1905 he urged frequent, even daily, Communion, and in 1910 he allowed children to receive their First Communion at the age of reason, about seven, instead of waiting until twelve or fourteen. He pressed for clear teaching of the catechism and began the work that produced the first Code of Canon Law in 1917.

He also led a hard campaign against what he called Modernism, ideas that he believed emptied the faith of its content. His encyclical Pascendi (1907) and the oath against Modernism (1910) were followed by suspicion and denunciations that harmed some loyal scholars, and historians today judge that side of his reign more critically. He died on 20 August 1914, just after the outbreak of the First World War, which he had tried to prevent. He asked to be buried simply. He was beatified in 1951 and canonized in 1954, the first pope canonized since Pius V in 1712. His body lies in St. Peter's Basilica.
One of the abbey's labels reads "B. Pius Pp. X" ("Blessed Pius, Pope, the Tenth"), which dates it between 1951 and 1954.
why_here: Three of Pius X's causes are lived at St. Bernard every day. The monks sing the Divine Office in choir, and the revival of Gregorian chant that he called for leaned heavily on Benedictine scholarship. Monks teach theology at the Prep, carrying on the catechesis he valued. And the youngest students, in seventh grade, belong to the first generations of Catholics who received Communion as children because he allowed it.

He is also a reminder that a holy man can be wrong in some of his methods. His campaign against error hurt good people. Honoring him honestly, as the abbey's four relics invite, means remembering both.
relic: Four relics: on the large grey linen board ("S. Pius Pp. X"), in a brass standing cross with flame-shaped rays ("S. Pius Pp. X"), in a silver flower-shaped frame ("S. Pius Pp. X"), and in a red leather case ("B. Pius Pp. X").

name: St. Radegund
title: Queen and nun, founder of Holy Cross, Poitiers
summary: Radegund was a Thuringian princess carried off as a child by the Franks and made a wife of King Clothar. She left him, founded the convent of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, and lived there as an ordinary nun, caring for the sick and lepers with her own hands. She is a patron of Poitiers, and a sister to monks who live under a Rule.
life: Radegund was a princess of Thuringia, in central Germany. In 531 the Frankish kings Theuderic and Clothar conquered her people, killed much of her family, and carried her off as part of the spoils. She was about eleven. Clothar had her raised and educated at a royal villa at Athies, in Picardy, and about 540 he made her one of his wives. We know her story well because two people who knew her wrote it down, the poet Venantius Fortunatus and a nun of her convent named Baudonivia, and St. Gregory of Tours, who buried her, also tells of her.

As queen she lived more like a nun than a royal wife. She fasted, prayed long into the night, and founded a house at Athies where she cared for the poor and the sick herself, washing and feeding them, including lepers whom others shunned. The court complained that the king had married a nun. About 550 Clothar had her younger brother, the last of her family, put to death. Radegund left him. At Noyon she went to Bishop Médard and asked to be consecrated to God, and when he hesitated, fearing the king, she put on a religious habit herself and insisted. He consecrated her a deaconess.

Clothar wanted her back, but in the end he gave way and even helped her found a convent at Poitiers. She made her friend Agnes abbess and lived there as an ordinary nun, under the rule written by St. Caesarius of Arles for nuns, doing her share of the cooking and cleaning. She never stopped working for peace among the Frankish kings, her husband's quarrelsome sons, writing to them and praying for them.

About 569 she obtained a relic of the True Cross from the Emperor Justin II in Constantinople, and the convent took the name of the Holy Cross. For its arrival Fortunatus, who lived nearby as her friend and later became bishop of Poitiers, wrote the hymns Vexilla Regis and Pange lingua gloriosi proelium, still sung in Holy Week. She died on 13 August 587 and was buried in the church now called Sainte-Radegonde in Poitiers.
The label "S. Radegundae R." means "of St. Radegund, Queen".
why_here: Radegund chose the common life of a convent over the court, and once there she asked for no special treatment. She lived by a rule, worked in the kitchen, and prayed the Office with her sisters. Monks who live under St. Benedict's Rule will recognize her life. Each Holy Week, when the hymns Fortunatus wrote for her relic of the Cross are sung, the Church is still singing her story.

She also cared for lepers with her own hands. The abbey remembers Fr. Urban Tracy, who served lepers, and Frater Hubert Carney, who died nursing others in 1918. Radegund belongs among those who did not keep the sick at a distance.
relic: One relic in the gold oval of royal saints and the House of Este, labeled "S. Radegundae R.".
check: Patronage of Jesus College, Cambridge rests on its founding on the site of St. Radegund's nunnery; drop it if only devotional patronages are wanted.
